Clackamas County in brief

About 1,884 square miles lie south and east of Portland in Clackamas County, with Oregon City as the seat and Lake Oswego as the biggest city. The land climbs from river-level suburbs to Mount Hood, so a Lake Oswego house, an Oregon City house and a cabin on the Mount Hood side sit in different markets and under different mixes of taxing districts, yet all of them appear on one county tax roll.

The 2020 Census counted 421,401 residents, the third-highest total in Oregon. Assessed value reached about $66.1 billion in fiscal year 2024-25. Old plats and long-held family parcels are common, so inherited houses with unclear paperwork turn up more often than you might expect.

Wet weather and what it does to houses

Oregon City gets 48.40 inches of precipitation a year. Houses here tend to show the same wear points: moss and worn granules on roofs, clogged gutters, wet crawl spaces with failing vapor barriers, decks, fences and siding that rot at the ground line, and trees that overhang the roof or lean toward the structure.

A house with several of these problems can be hard to list the usual way. Plenty of owners skip the repair bills and sell the house as it is.

Clackamas County tax figures and contacts

Taxing districts imposed about $1.17 billion in property tax for fiscal year 2024-25 on $66.15 billion of assessed value. The average rate was $17.68 per $1,000 of assessed value, and the Measure 5 rate was $9.82 per $1,000 of Measure 5 value. What you pay turns on the specific districts at your address.

HoursOpen Monday through Thursday, 8 a.m. until 4 p.m.

Why your bill does not follow the sale price

Tax is figured on the smaller of a home's real market value and its maximum assessed value, so a rising market does not by itself push a bill up. Under Measure 50, every property's 1997-98 assessed value was set back to 90% of its 1995-96 figure, and yearly growth after that stops at 3%.

The cap has exceptions for new construction, remodeling, new subdivisions and rezoning. A buyer who adds square footage can see assessed value jump on that portion.

Measure 5 runs on a separate track. It limits education taxes to $5 and general government taxes to $10 per $1,000 of real market value. Anything above the limit is compressed, with local option levies cut first. A lower market value lowers taxes only if it falls below assessed value, so many owners see no change after a successful appeal.

Paying the bill

You can pay by mail, online, through bank bill pay, in person at Room 135 in Oregon City, or in the drop box at the front of the building. Make checks out to Clackamas County Tax, and do not mail cash.

Online payments run through US Bank at apps.clackamas.us/pay/at. An e-check costs $3, credit cards and MasterCard debit cost 2.49%, and Visa debit costs $3.95. Bank bill pay is handled by your bank, can take several business days and counts only when the county posts it.

Three due dates apply: November 15, February 15 and May 15. A weekend or holiday pushes the date to the next business day. Settle the whole bill by November 15 and you get a 3% discount.

The office does not take prepayment of taxes a district has not certified, except in cases the law allows, such as recording a subdivision or moving a manufactured home. Money is applied to the oldest year first, so a seller who is two years behind cannot target the newer one.

Unpaid taxes and foreclosure

Real property tax is delinquent after May 15, and foreclosure starts once taxes have been late for three years. A statement marks an account facing foreclosure with an asterisk.

Under ORS chapter 312, a foreclosed property is held for two years, and during that period these people can redeem it:

  • anyone who held an interest on the judgment date, and their heirs or devisees
  • anyone with a recorded lien on the property
  • a city or district with a lien on it

To redeem, an owner pays the full judgment with interest, a 5% penalty and a fee. With no redemption, the county receives the deed from the tax collector. Equity above the debt is at stake here, not only the tax bill, which is the strongest reason to sell before a judgment instead of after.

Watch your statement for the asterisk. If you see it, call the office the same week and ask exactly which years are late and what has to be paid to stop the clock.

How to appeal your value

The Property Value Appeals Board hears appeals, and petitions go to the County Clerk by December 31. Clerk staff at 503-655-8662 can send petition forms, and Assessment and Taxation at 503-655-8671 can talk through the value before you file.

The clerk takes petitions once statements are out. Hearings open on or after the first Monday in February, and the board finishes by March 15.

Measure 5 and Measure 50 limit most bills, so an appeal changes the amount mostly when real market value sits close to assessed value, or when the property was valued with features it does not have. Photos, an appraisal and sales near January 1 give the board something concrete.

What to settle before closing

First, the tax year. It runs July 1 through June 30 with the lien attaching July 1. Have escrow show how this year gets divided and confirm no older year is owed.

Next, look for a senior or disabled deferral. Qualifying owners have the state pay the county, with a 6% lien recorded against the house. Selling or transferring the home ends the program, and the balance, interest and recording costs come due by August 15 of the next year. Heirs can be on the hook too.

Last, prepare the seller disclosure. ORS 105.464 gives the buyer five days to revoke after getting it. Court-appointed personal representatives and foreclosing financial institutions can claim an exclusion.

Records to collect before you list

Pull the parcel from the county's online records and write down its real market value, its maximum assessed value and the districts that bill it. Check the statement for an asterisk, and ask whether any deferral lien is recorded. These three items tell a buyer's lender and the escrow officer what to expect at the table.

For a Lake Oswego house the questions will differ from those on a Mount Hood cabin, so tell the escrow officer early which kind of property you are selling and whether wells, septic or private roads are involved.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Being behind does not stop a cash sale. The county supplies a payoff figure, the title company deducts it from your proceeds at the table, and the new deed gets recorded. Ask for the payoff broken out by year if more than one is open.

Call Assessment and Taxation before you choose how to sell. Find out how far behind the account is, whether a deferral lien exists, and what the payoff would be on the closing date you want. Then compare a listing, which needs repairs, showings and time, against a written offer that settles everything at the title company.

Frequently asked questions

When are Clackamas County property taxes due?

Bills are due November 15, February 15 and May 15, and the date shifts to the next business day when it falls on a weekend or holiday. Paying in full by November 15 earns a 3% discount.

How do I contact Clackamas County Assessment and Taxation?

Call 503-655-8671 or email propertytaxinfo@clackamas.us. The office is at 150 Beavercreek Road, Room 135, Oregon City, and keeps Monday to Thursday hours from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Does Clackamas County foreclose on unpaid property taxes?

Yes. Foreclosure begins after taxes have been delinquent for three years, and the owner then has a two-year redemption period after the judgment. Unredeemed property is deeded to the county.

Can I lower my Clackamas County property tax by appealing?

Sometimes. Because taxes follow the lower of market value and assessed value, a lower market value only helps if it drops below assessed value. File with the County Clerk by December 31.

What do I owe if I sell a house with a deferred property tax lien?

You owe the deferred taxes, 6% annual interest and recording costs. The state program makes the balance due by August 15 of the year after a sale or ownership change.

Lane County in brief

Lane County stretches from the Pacific coast to the Cascade crest, with Eugene as its seat. At 4,722 square miles it is one of just two Oregon counties that reach from ocean to mountains. The 2020 census counted 382,971 people, the fourth largest total in the state, and Eugene and Springfield hold 176,654 and 61,851 of them.

Roughly 82% of residents live in urban areas. Everyone else is scattered through small places such as Dexter, Marcola, Mapleton, Lorane, Blachly and McKenzie Bridge, where a house often depends on a well, a septic system and a rural fire district. Those details shape a sale, because buyers of rural homes ask about them first.

How the tax roll and levies work

Lane County certified about $746 million in property tax for 2025 to 2026, roughly 3.49% above the prior year. The 182,937 accounts sit inside 85 taxing districts: cities, schools, water, fire, urban renewal, parks, libraries and ambulance districts. Most accounts are homes. Residential or tract property makes up 54.2% of the roll, exempt property 16.2%, commercial 9.21%, industrial 6.59%, multifamily 5.46% and farm and forest 4.17%.

Values are set as of January 1 from the prior year's sales. A sale or refinance does not reset assessed value in Oregon. Maximum assessed value generally climbs 3% a year, and rate limits cap general government at $10 per $1,000 of market value and schools at $5, with bonds sitting outside those caps.

Your address decides which local levies you pay. The 2025 statements carried a new five-year Lowell Rural Fire Protection District levy of $1.50 per $1,000 of assessed value, and the McKenzie Rural Fire Protection District levy went to $1.05 from $0.60. Two houses of equal value can therefore owe different amounts.

Due dates and discounts

Lane County follows the standard Oregon schedule. Paying the whole bill by November 15 earns a 3% discount, paying two-thirds earns 2%, and at least one-third must be paid to stay clear of interest. When November 15 lands on a weekend, the deadline moves to the next business day.

Statements are mailed and also posted on the county's Assessment and Taxation pages. The county's property lookup shows the account and its breakdown by district. Before you talk to any buyer, open the account for your house and save a screenshot of the balance.

Fire-damaged and McKenzie corridor lots

The Holiday Farm Fire burned from September 7 to October 29, 2020, and consumed 173,393 acres along the McKenzie River. Most structures in Blue River were destroyed, and many properties in nearby communities were lost. Owners of rebuilt homes or vacant lots in that corridor often have value questions, so start with the Assessor.

The Property Value Appeals Board can also review values adjusted for destroyed or damaged property. Near the coast, houses face heavy moisture. Florence averages about 75.52 inches of precipitation a year, so buyers there look hard at moss, decay and ventilation.

How to appeal your property value

If the market value looks wrong, call the Assessor's Office at 541-682-4321 first. Should that fail, file a petition with the Property Value Appeals Board (PVAB). It is staffed through Lane County Deeds and Records at 125 East 8th Avenue, Eugene.

  • Deadline for the 2026 tax year: December 31, 2026, at 4:00 pm for hand delivery, or postmarked by that date.
  • Filing opens the day after tax statements are mailed.
  • Fee: $35.00 per tax account, capped at $350.00 for several accounts with the same owner and subdivision.
  • Hearings run on Zoom, starting on or after the first Monday in February 2027 and ending by April 15, 2027.
  • Evidence is due at least two business days before your hearing.

PVAB hears questions of value only, not disputes over the amount of tax billed. A further appeal goes to the Oregon Tax Court Magistrate Division within 30 days of the order. Forms are on the county's appeals page.

Recording a deed

Lane County Deeds and Records charges $102 to record a one-page, one-title document, with $5 for each added page. That covers deeds, deeds of trust, mortgages and easements. The total includes a Public Land Corner Preservation Fee of $25 per document under House Bill 3175.

You can pay by check or money order, by card (a 3% bank fee applies) or with cash in person. A document sent with too little money comes back unrecorded, so add a cushion for a multi-page deed.

Selling with taxes owed or a house that needs work

Oregon lets a county foreclose on real property once the earliest delinquency is three years old. After judgment the county holds the property for two years, and the owner or a lienholder can redeem during that window.

Lane County sellers often arrive with other burdens as well: an inherited house on a rural lot, roof work put off for years, tenants in place, or a lien. The order of work is the same each time:

  • Get the tax balance from the county.
  • Get the payoff for any lien.
  • Compare offers that do not ask you to make repairs first.

The state's deferral program for qualifying senior and disabled owners leaves a lien too, and that lien must be paid when the house sells.

What a cash sale skips

A cash buyer does not wait on a lender appraisal, so a house with old roofing, a worn crawlspace or an out-of-date septic system is not held up by repair conditions. The tax balance and any lien payoff still get paid from the proceeds at closing, and the title company handles that. Ask the buyer for a closing date that leaves time to collect the county balance and any payoff letters, and bring your deed information and a photo ID to the signing.

A simple order of events helps. First, pull the account and screenshot the balance. Second, ask the Assessor whether the value looks right, especially for a rebuilt or fire-affected lot, and file with PVAB before December 31 if it does not. Third, line up the deed for recording, and check the page count so the fee is right. Fourth, confirm with the title company which tax years are open, so nothing is left unpaid after the sale funds.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Lane County, Oregon property tax appeal deadline?

For the 2026 tax year it is December 31, 2026, at 4:00 pm for hand delivery or postmarked by that date. File with the Property Value Appeals Board at Lane County Deeds and Records, 125 East 8th Avenue, Eugene.

How much does an appeal of a Lane County property value cost?

The fee is $35.00 per tax account. For several accounts with the same owner in one subdivision, it tops out at $350.00.

Can the appeals board lower my Lane County tax bill?

It can change the property value, not the bill itself. A lower value does not always lead to a refund.

Is there an early payment discount in Lane County?

Yes. Paying in full by November 15 takes off 3%, and paying two-thirds takes off 2%. At least one-third has to be paid to avoid interest.

Does selling a Lane County house reset its assessed value?

No. Oregon does not reset values at sale or refinancing, and maximum assessed value generally rises 3% a year unless there is new construction or a similar change.

Linn County in brief

The middle of the Willamette Valley belongs to Linn County, whose seat, Albany, is also its biggest city. The 2020 census counted 128,610 residents, a 10.2% gain over 2010, across 2,309 square miles. The county was created on December 28, 1847. Housing units numbered 51,921 in 2020, and 66.1% were owner-occupied.

Towns include Albany, Lebanon, Sweet Home, Brownsville, Harrisburg, Halsey, Scio, Tangent, Millersburg, Lyons and Sodaville, plus parts of Gates, Idanha and Mill City. About 34.2% of residents live in rural areas, so plenty of sellers own acreage, a shop or a farm house.

Where your tax dollar goes

Schools take the largest share. For the 2024 assessment year, the county's notice split the tax this way:

  • Schools: 41.7%
  • County: 23.5%
  • Cities: 23%
  • Rural fire districts: 7%
  • Urban renewal: 3.2%
  • Miscellaneous: 1.6%

Voters also approved changes in several districts. Jefferson Rural Fire District added a local option levy of $0.81 per $1,000 of assessed value, and Sweet Home Fire and Ambulance District set a new bond rate of $0.46 per $1,000. How and when to pay

Statements arrive by October 25. A full payment received by November 15 saves 3%. Two-thirds by that date saves 2%, and the last third is due May 15. Splitting the bill into thirds saves nothing and means paying in November, February and May. No reminder comes for the February or May installments, and a statement under $40 has to be paid all at once.

  • By mail: check or money order to Linn County Tax Collector, PO Box 100, Albany, OR 97321. Cash should never go in the mail.
  • In person: Room 214, Linn County Courthouse, 300 4th Avenue SW, Albany.
  • Drop box: courthouse west (Ferry Street) entrance, left of the doors.
  • Online: card or e-check.

A postmark counts toward the discount, but a returned check can forfeit it. Payments go to the earliest year still owed.

Delinquent taxes and foreclosure

Delinquency notices go out between May 16 and May 25. A property that has been delinquent for three years lands on the foreclosure list around July 16. The list is usually published around August 16, and final judgment follows around September 16. The oldest delinquent year has to be paid to pull a property off the list.

Two years of redemption follow judgment. An owner who redeems pays the taxes, a 5% penalty, interest and a fee, and any surplus above the debt belongs to the owner after the county takes the property.

For a payoff figure, call 541-967-3808 during business hours. A title company will ask for it before closing on a Linn County sale.

Recording rules at the Clerk's office

The Clerk records deeds from 8:30 AM to 4:00 PM at 300 4th Ave. SW in Albany. Anything received between 4:00 and 5:00 PM is recorded the next business day.

How to challenge your value

If you think the market value on your statement is too high, call the Assessor at 541-967-3808 first. Many questions get answered with one conversation, and the staff can explain how the figure was reached for your parcel. If you still disagree, the Property Value Appeal Board is the place to file, and the deadline is December 31. Do not wait for the last week, because you will want time to gather sales of similar houses and photos of any defects. Keep a copy of everything you send, and write down the date and time of any call you make to the office.

Farm parcels and deferral

Farm use is taxed under a special assessment that values land by income instead of market value. Disqualified land can owe extra tax for up to 10 years, or five inside an urban growth boundary. Ending farm use, leaving an exclusive farm use zone, or approval of a nonfarm dwelling can trigger it.

Ask the Linn County Assessor for the special assessment status before you list rural land. Senior and disabled owners can also ask about the state's deferral program, which leaves a lien that is repaid at sale. The county keeps a page on the Senior or Disabled Citizen Deferral program.

Wildfire and wet-season wear on homes

Albany gets about 39.89 inches of precipitation a year, with December the wettest month. Sweet Home, nearer the Cascades, gets about 54.45 inches, mostly from October through March, so moss, drainage and crawlspace moisture are the usual inspection items there.

Wildfire touched the eastern edge of the county in 2020. The Santiam Fire burned 402,274 acres across Marion, Linn, Jefferson and Clackamas counties. Detroit and Gates were nearly destroyed, Idanha and Mill City were damaged, and more than 1,500 structures were lost.

Selling a Linn County house with a tax balance

A balance does not stop a sale. Here is the usual path:

  • Call the Assessor at 541-967-3808 for a payoff figure.
  • Give the figure to the title company.
  • Escrow pays the oldest year first, because payments are credited that way, and settles the rest from your proceeds.

A cash buyer skips lender appraisals and repair conditions, which helps when a farm house or a shop has deferred work. Bring your deed, the latest statement and, for acreage, the special assessment status to your first meeting. Plan the calendar around the payment dates. A closing in late October or early November means the November 15 installment is about to come due, so settle in the contract who pays it. A closing in spring puts the May 15 installment in play, and the Tax Collector sends no reminder for it.

What is the county seat of Linn County, Oregon?

Albany, which is also the largest city. An 1851 territorial act moved the seat there, and a special election in 1856 confirmed it.

When are Linn County property taxes due?

November 15 for a full payment or the first installment. The remaining installments are due February 15 and May 15, and statements are mailed by October 25.

How do I pay Linn County property tax in person?

Go to Room 214 of the Linn County Courthouse, 300 4th Avenue SW in Albany, or use the drop box at the west (Ferry Street) entrance. Checks go to Linn County Tax Collector.

When is the Linn County property tax appeal deadline?

December 31. File with the Property Value Appeal Board, and call the Assessor at 541-967-3808 with questions first.

How long can Linn County taxes go unpaid before foreclosure?

Marion County in brief

About 1,194 square miles of the Willamette Valley make up Marion County. Salem serves as seat, biggest city and state capital. Population was 345,920 in 2020, fifth highest among Oregon counties. Your house might be minutes from the capitol or well out on a country road, but one assessor values it and one tax collector bills it either way.

Its history goes back to July 5, 1843, when it started as the Champooick District. Agriculture and food processing are big here, including 10,640 acres of orchards, and government is the other anchor: the State of Oregon, Salem Health and the Salem-Keizer School District are the biggest local employers. Steady public employment tends to keep housing demand even.

How your tax bill is figured

Your bill rests on assessed value, and that figure usually trails real market value. Measure 50 holds yearly growth on existing property to 3 percent, with assessed value never allowed past market value. Measure 5 sets ceilings of $10 per $1,000 of real market value for general government and $5 per $1,000 for schools. A bill that would break a ceiling gets trimmed, a step called compression, and local option taxes are trimmed first. For most properties compression has a minimal effect.

  • Real market value: the assessor's guess at a selling price.
  • Assessed value: the base the rates multiply, valued differently for new construction.
  • Each taxing district appears on the statement, since county, city, school and special district rates pile onto one bill.

A sale price can run far above the assessed value, and the two are unrelated figures.

Due dates and payment options

The county mails about 124,000 statements from October 15 to October 25. November 15 is the big deadline. No bill by November 1? Phone the tax department.

Send payment to the Marion County Tax Collection Department by mail, use the county's Paystation page online or by phone, or go to Courthouse Square, 555 Court Street NE in Salem. After hours, use the drop boxes at the main entrance or the second-floor elevator lobby.

How to appeal your assessment

Two dates matter. Ask for an informal review by December 10, and file a formal petition with the Property Value Appeals Board by December 31. The review is optional and is no appeal, yet an appraiser will recheck the property and records, which may settle things without a petition.

  1. Ask for a review online once October statements are out. Real property and business personal property have their own forms.
  2. Submit one petition per account to the Marion County Clerk's Office. The Clerk takes hand delivery until 5 p.m., email and fax until midnight on December 31, and mail postmarked by that date.
  3. Go to a hearing lasting about 15 minutes. You get notice 5 to 10 days ahead, the decision comes at the hearing, and the written order arrives within 8 to 10 business days.
  4. Still disagree? Send a written complaint to the Oregon Tax Court Magistrate Division within 30 days after the order is mailed.
  5. The magistrate's ruling can go to the Regular Division within 60 days.

Your evidence should show what the property was worth on January 1 of the assessment year. Hearings happen on the second floor at Courthouse Square, and you can arrange video or phone ahead of time. Call the Clerk at (503) 588-3578 or the Assessor at (503) 588-5144.

Selling with taxes owed

Foreclosure must begin when a property's oldest unpaid year reaches three years delinquent. Tax turns delinquent each May 16, and that is when the clock starts for the year.

  • June: delinquent notices say when foreclosure would start.
  • July and August: owners get letters, and from then on payment must be cash or a cashier's check.
  • August 16 or later: the list is published, the county asks circuit court for judgment, and a 5 percent penalty joins the tax and interest.
  • About 30 days after publication: judgment is granted and redemption runs for two years.
  • Two years after judgment: redemption ends and the county takes the deed.

In redemption, only people with a recorded interest on the judgment date may pay, and partial payments are refused. Reach the tax office at 503-588-5215 or propertytax@co.marion.or.us. Owners who are behind and cannot catch up may consider a quick sale ahead of publication, when the cost jumps.

Taxes at closing

Before you sign a sale contract, get the current balance and any delinquent years from the tax office. Older years are paid first. Escrow or the title company decides the buyer and seller split of tax on the settlement statement.

  • Find your latest statement and check the account number and mailing address.
  • See whether your mortgage servicer pays through an impound account.
  • Give the county a mailing address that still works after the sale.
  • Warn the title company about unpaid years so the payoff is right.

The County Clerk's records office records deeds under its own fee schedule and first-page rules, and a deed that misses them can draw a cover sheet fee.

Think about timing before you list. If your closing falls near November 15, ask who will make that installment. If you sell during the spring, the May 15 installment may still be open. Either way, a current statement in hand lets the title company check what remains for the year. Cash buyers can often close on a date that suits your schedule, which helps a relocating state or school employee or an heir who lives out of the area and wants the house sold without making repairs.

Weather, wildfire and older homes

Salem has mild, damp weather, around 40 inches of precipitation yearly, nearly all of it October through April. Roofs, gutters, crawl spaces and siding take the toll. Financed buyers often request repairs there, and some sellers avoid that by selling as-is.

The 2020 Santiam Fire complex burned 402,274 acres and wiped out nearly all of Detroit. Anyone with damaged or vacant canyon land may face questions on insurance, rebuilding and assessed value. The assessor can explain how your statement value was set.

When is Marion County property tax due?

November 15 is the main date. A full payment by then saves 3 percent, and two-thirds saves 2 percent with the rest due May 15. One-third plans have February 15 and May 15 installments and no discount.

What is the last day to appeal a Marion County value?

December 31, filed with the Marion County Clerk's Office. The optional informal review request is due December 10. A weekend or holiday on December 31 pushes the deadline to the next business day.

Where does a Marion County tax payment go?

Mail it to Marion County Tax Collection Dept., PO Box 3416, Portland, OR 97208-3416, postmarked by the due date, or use the county's Paystation page. To pay in person, go to Courthouse Square, 555 Court Street NE, Salem.

How long before Marion County can foreclose for unpaid tax?

It begins once the oldest unpaid year is three years delinquent. Judgment is followed by two years of redemption, after which an unredeemed property is deeded to the county.

Can I sell my Marion County house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The back taxes are paid from the sale money at closing, oldest year first. Request a payoff figure from the tax office and pass it to escrow.

About Polk County

Polk County lies in western Oregon, just west of Salem. Marion County lies across the Willamette on the east, and the valley fills the eastern half of Polk. The county seat is Dallas. Roughly 90,037 people lived here in mid-2025, in 36,026 housing units, 64.7% of them owner-occupied. A typical owner-occupied home was worth $454,700 for 2020 to 2024. Forest covers roughly the western two-thirds, so sellers here may hold a valley lot near Salem or a timber parcel toward the Coast Range. Use that figure loosely, since a farm outside Rickreall and a Monmouth house can land far from it.

Which office does what

The job is shared. Value is the Assessor's call. The Tax and Finance Office, 850 Main Street, Dallas, Oregon 97338, sends bills and takes payments. For an appeal, get forms from the County Clerk and file with the Property Value Appeals Board.

Late October brings the statements. They come in four kinds (real, personal, manufactured structure and utility), each for the July 1 to June 30 tax year. A note in the information section shows when a mortgage company requested the bill. Online, the county offers an account lookup and a contact form.

At a sale, the title or escrow company checks the account, then splits the current year between you and the buyer on the settlement statement. Request the status early. An installment you forgot can surface as an unwelcome payoff line.

How assessed values are capped

Tax is levied on assessed value, whichever is lower of real market value and maximum assessed value. The maximum climbs 3% a year at most, unless there is new construction, a major remodel, rezoning or a new lot.

Measure 5 sets its own ceilings tied to real market value: $5 per $1,000 for education and $10 per $1,000 for general government. Voter-approved bonds usually sit outside them, and local option levies are trimmed first when a category goes over.

So an owner of many years can pay far less than someone who just bought a similar home. And a market value cut will not always cut the tax if assessed value was already lower.

Timing a Polk County sale around the tax calendar

Use the calendar when choosing a listing date. A closing just ahead of November 15 means the first installment is nearly due, and a spring closing bumps against the April 1 exemption deadline and the May 15 third payment. Dallas, Monmouth, Independence and Falls City

The four cities differ in size and setting.

  • Monmouth: 11,110 residents in 2020, about 12 miles west of Salem on Oregon Route 99W, home to Western Oregon University.
  • Independence: 9,828 residents in 2020, on the west bank of the Willamette River. A December 1861 flood wiped out its commercial district and farms.
  • Falls City: 1,051 residents in 2020, in the Coast Range hills with the Little Luckiamute River through its center.

Homes close to the Willamette or a creek should get a flood-risk review before listing. After wet winters, buyers go straight to roofs, gutters and crawl space moisture.

Which office collects Polk County property tax?

The Tax and Finance Office, 850 Main Street in Dallas. Values come from the Assessor.

By December 31 (next business day if that is a weekend or holiday). The board hears cases from the first Monday in February to April 15.

Three years after the delinquency date, with taxes unpaid after May 15 counting as delinquent. Judgment is followed by two years to redeem.

Douglas County overview

Three years of delinquency opens the door to foreclosure on real property, and after judgment the owner gets two years to redeem. ORS chapter 312 lets recorded interest holders, their heirs and lien holders redeem. The price is the judgment amount, interest, a 5% penalty and a fee.

Seniors may be in the state deferral program, which places a lien at 6% interest. Selling the house ends the deferral. The unpaid balance must then be paid by August 15 of the following year, and heirs can be liable if the owner has died.

Oregon's seller disclosure form (ORS 105.464) travels with a written offer. After receiving it the buyer has five days to revoke. A personal representative or a financial institution that foreclosed may complete only part of the form.

Long distances between towns mean a buyer may drive a long way to see your house, so the details need to be ready. Know the water source, the septic status and how the road is maintained. Say whether any part of the land is in a farm or forest program.

Jackson County overview

Jackson County runs along the California line in southern Oregon, with Medford as its seat. It covers 2,802 square miles and had 223,259 people in 2020, most of them in the Rogue Valley along the Bear Creek corridor that links Ashland, Talent, Phoenix, Medford and Central Point. Medford itself had 85,824.

The county has 11 incorporated cities and 34 unincorporated communities. A house can sit inside a city, in a small community with its own fire district, or on rural land outside any city, and the taxing districts on the bill change from one address to the next.

Health care, orchards, wine, a university and a theater festival bring in varied buyers, from hospital staff to retirees to orchard and vineyard owners. Condition and location still drive price more than any single employer.

Heat, fire and what they mean for a house

Medford has a dry Mediterranean climate, about 18.43 inches of precipitation a year, and the wear on a roof and cooling system shows it. The city averages about 61 afternoons above 90 degrees Fahrenheit and 11 above 100 each year. Winter is mild but not frost free, with freezing mornings on roughly 64 days a year.

Fire is the larger risk. The Almeda Drive Fire started on September 8, 2020, near Ashland and reached Phoenix and Talent within hours. It burned about 3,200 acres and destroyed more than 3,000 structures. Houses that were damaged, rebuilt or left vacant afterward often come with unusual tax and insurance questions.

If your Jackson County property was damaged, ask the Assessor's Office how the loss is reflected in its value before you set a price.

Who handles property tax

Property tax here splits between two county offices. The Assessor's Office values property, keeps the maps and ownership records, handles exemptions and oversees farm and forest special assessments. The Taxation office in the Finance Department collects the money.

The Assessor values residential, commercial and business personal property, plus industrial land and improvements under $1,000,000, and verifies sales to track the market. The county also posts a Summary of Assessment and Levies report each fall.

Due dates and early-payment discounts

Everything starts on November 15, and settling the whole bill by that day earns a 3% discount. Statements are sent by October 25. If the 15th is a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, you get until the next business day. Ask the office to confirm the date in those years.

  • Whole bill by November 15: you save 3%.
  • Pay two-thirds by that date: you save 2%, and the remainder is due May 15.
  • One-third by that date: no discount, then more is due February 15 and May 15.
  • Interest of 1.333% a month (16% a year) starts on December 16, February 16 and May 16 for the three installments.

Mailed checks need a postmark dated on or before the due date, but mail consolidation means a local postmark may never be applied, which is a risk close to the deadline. Drop boxes are open around the clock, and payments there are credited the same day. Payments go first to fees, then to the oldest tax year owed.

Paying online by credit card adds a processor fee of 2.40% with a $2.00 minimum. Debit is 1% with the same minimum, and an e-check is $2.50. The county receives no part of those fees. Your petition is filed with the Property Value Appeals Board clerk. You can file once your tax statement arrives, up to December 31 (the next business day if that is a weekend or holiday).

If you lose before the board, the Oregon Tax Court Magistrate Division is next, and a value appeal has a 30 day clock. Appeals about exemptions, special assessment disqualification or omitted property have a 90 day window. The Magistrate Division is at 1163 State St, Salem.

An appeal changes value only. It does not erase a bill that is already due, so a seller facing a closing date should pay what the county asks and treat any refund as a later matter.

If taxes go unpaid

Delinquent notices go out by mail in mid-June, with 1.333% monthly interest on every missed installment. ORS 312.010 allows foreclosure on real property when three years have gone by since the earliest delinquency date.

Once a judgment is entered, the property stays on hold for two years. Redeeming in that window costs the judgment amount, interest, a 5% penalty and a fee, and either the owner or a lienholder may pay it. Should the property be worth more than the debt, the owner is due the surplus after the county takes it.

Selling is one way to stop that clock. A cash sale can pay the old years out of proceeds at closing, and the Taxation office at 541-774-6541 can give you the balance for each year.

Jackson County charges $99.00 for a one-page deed (bargain and sale, quitclaim, warranty or transfer on death), with $5.00 for each added page. A trust deed or mortgage is $116.00. Call the Clerk at 541-774-6152 to confirm the current amount.

A document missing required first-page information carries a $20.00 non-standard fee. Regular copies are $4.00 for the first page, and certified copies are $7.75.

Start with the tax account, then the land. A few checks save the most trouble:

  • Confirm whether the parcel has a farm or forest special assessment, since ending that use can trigger extra tax.
  • Ask whether any special assessment, fee or charge is attached to the account.
  • For fire-damaged or rebuilt property, ask the Assessor how the value was set.

Land that loses farm status can owe extra tax going back up to 10 years, or five inside an urban growth boundary. Rogue Valley orchard and vineyard parcels are exactly the type of land this affects.

Once you take an offer, the title company orders a tax report and asks Taxation for a payoff on each open year. They will want the deed, any deferral paperwork, and for an inherited house, proof of who has authority to sign.

At the closing table your proceeds cover the old years, interest and any special charge, and the Clerk's office records the new deed. Leave a few days for a deferral lien, because the state release is separate from the county payoff and can take weeks to post.

Senior deferral liens

Seniors and disabled owners sometimes use the state deferral program. The Department of Revenue pays the county on the owner's behalf and records a lien, which must be repaid, with 6% simple interest, before it is released. A deferral account therefore has a payoff figure at closing, and release takes about eight weeks after payment posts.

What is the county seat of Jackson County, Oregon?

Medford. Jacksonville was the first seat in 1853, and the seat moved to Medford in 1927 after the railroad bypassed Jacksonville.

How much is the early payment discount on Jackson County property tax?

It is 3% for paying in full by November 15, and 2% for paying two-thirds by that date. The one-third plan has no discount.

What is the Jackson County property tax appeal deadline?

December 31, filed with the Property Value Appeals Board after you receive your statement. If that date is a weekend or holiday, the next business day applies.

At Room 111A, 10 S Oakdale Ave, Medford, Monday through Friday from 8 AM to 4 PM. Drop boxes are open 24 hours a day, and the phone number is 541-774-6541.

Can I sell a Jackson County house with back taxes owed?

Yes. The unpaid years are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Call the Taxation office for the balance of each year, because payments are applied to the oldest year first and interest is 1.333% a month.

Hillsboro is the seat of Washington County, which lies about 20 miles west of Portland and ranks second in Oregon by population (611,708 in the 2025 estimate). Where the money goes

One tax dollar divides as follows, with schools getting the largest share:

  • Education: 47.38 cents
  • Cities and special districts: 32.42 cents
  • Washington County: 16.82 cents
  • Regional governments: 3.38 cents

Permanent rates date to 1995 and are set at $5 per $1,000 of real market value for schools and $10 per $1,000 for general government. Voters can add bonds and local option levies on top. Hillsboro has a police, fire and parks levy, for instance, and Beaverton has a school levy for teachers. Levies vary by district, so identical houses can carry unequal bills.

RMV, MAV and assessed value

The bill starts from assessed value, meaning whichever is smaller: real market value (RMV) or maximum assessed value (MAV). The assessor sets RMV as the likely sale price on January 1, and RMV itself has no cap.

MAV grows at most 3% annually. Even so, a bill can jump further when a district passes a new bond or local option levy, or when major renovations were finished before January 1.

The county mails statements by October 25 and expects payment November 15. You can pay everything or take thirds, and full payment that is postmarked or received by the deadline earns 3% off.

  • At the counter or the drop box at the Public Services Building.

The color of the statement tells you who is paying. Green means the owner handles the bill. Yellow means a mortgage company or the Oregon Department of Revenue requested it, so after a purchase, sale or refinance, check with the lender that payment will continue. Past-due money shows on the statement and goes to the oldest year first. An asterisk beside a year marks foreclosure proceedings.

How to appeal your assessment

Disagree with the value? File a petition with the Property Value Appeals Board, which used to be named the Board of Property Tax Appeals. Petitions are accepted from the day statements go in the mail through December 31. Washington County asks for no fee, and a lawyer is optional.

  • Hearings are held from the first Monday in February to April 15; showing up is your choice.
  • Bring a recent sale, a fee appraisal or comparable homes near January 1.
  • Still unhappy after the ruling? The Magistrate Division of the Oregon Tax Court hears the next round. Filing costs $50 and must happen within 30 days of the board’s order.

Real estate transfer tax

The county levies a transfer tax on sales: one dollar for every thousand of the price. Buyer and seller share the liability.

Pay it, or file a claim for exemption, within 15 days after the deed is recorded. Waiting longer triggers a penalty. The county publishes exemption forms for these cases:

  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure and court-ordered transfers
  • Trustee’s deeds from foreclosure
  • Gifts, devises and inheritances
  • Transfers between spouses under a dissolution or separation order
  • Sales under $13,999

The Recording Division at the Hillsboro address processes these. A house you inherited is treated differently from a plain sale, so your title company should tell you which form to file.

Splitting taxes at closing

Escrow does the arithmetic, and the answer turns on when you close. The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30. If you close between July 1 and mid-October, the buyer will owe the coming bill, so you give the buyer a credit for your share, figured from last year’s tax.

If you close between mid-October and June 30, the bill has typically been paid by you already, and the buyer repays you for the stretch after the agreed transfer date. Escrow also requests payoff figures for liens. Money liens are usually settled from the proceeds, which leaves the buyer with clear title.

Selling with taxes or a deferral lien owed

Back taxes and deferral liens are paid out of the proceeds or cleared before closing, so learn the balance early. Two state programs, the Senior Citizen’s Deferral (age 62 or older) and the Disabled Citizen’s Deferral, let the Department of Revenue pay your tax in exchange for a lien and 6% interest. That money comes due later. A deferred account is flagged at the bottom of the statement.

Tax foreclosure moves slowly but it does happen. ORS 312.010 lets the county foreclose after three years of delinquency, counted from the earliest unpaid year. ORS 312.120 gives owners two more years after judgment to redeem. The county may keep, transfer or auction what it takes. If you are behind, a sale before judgment leaves the house with you.

Start with your latest statement: note its color, the balance, and any asterisk on an earlier year. If the figures look off, call the payment line. Ask the appeals line whether a value petition makes sense before December 31. It is one dollar per thousand dollars of selling price, and buyer and seller share liability. You must pay it or file an exemption claim within 15 days of the recording date.

File a petition with the Property Value Appeals Board between the date statements are mailed and December 31. There is no filing fee in Washington County, and the appeals line is 503-846-3854.

A yellow statement means a mortgage company or the Oregon Department of Revenue requested the bill. If you recently bought, sold or refinanced, confirm with your lender that the tax will still be paid.

Two large blocks of land limit what can be owned here. Crooked River Ranch is the largest unincorporated community, a census-designated place with 4,912 people in southern Jefferson County, between the Deschutes and Crooked rivers near Lake Billy Chinook. Its roughly 12,000 acres make it the biggest homeowner association in Oregon.

Who collects property tax

One office, the Finance Department, sends the bills and takes the money for every district that taxes Jefferson County property. You will find it at 66 SE D Street, Suite E, Madras. The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30. Bills are mailed by October 25. Installments fall on November 15, February 15 and May 15, and a date that hits a weekend or holiday slides to the next business day.

ORS 311.505 creates the discounts. Settle the whole bill in November and the county knocks off 3%. Send two-thirds and you get 2%. Send less and you get nothing.

After judgment the owner gets two years to redeem. An heir, a recorded lienholder or a city with a lien may also step in, paying the taxes, interest, penalty and a fee. If the house sells for more than the debt, the extra belongs to the owner.

You can still sell while owing tax. The usual sequence:

  • Hand it to the buyer's title company.

Down in the Willamette Valley, Benton County spans 679 square miles. Corvallis is where the county government sits, and it is also the largest town. Adair Village, Monroe and Philomath are the other towns, and a sliver of Albany reaches in from Linn County.

Oregon State University drives the local economy, with help from agriculture, forest products, electronics and wineries. Fall 2024 enrollment reached 37,900 students, 24,900 of them in Corvallis. Many houses near campus belong to landlords, estates or relatives living elsewhere, so tenants and distant heirs come up often in sales.

Corvallis sees 42.71 inches of precipitation a year, mostly as winter rain. Months of damp hit the same spots on most houses: roof surface and gutters, crawl space moisture, siding and decks, and grading around the foundation. Buyer inspectors check them first.

Benton County tax figures

In fiscal 2024-25, about $198.5 million in tax was imposed on $11.13 billion of assessed value. The county's average rate was $17.83 per $1,000, and its Measure 5 rate was $9.45 per $1,000 of Measure 5 value.

For a bill or a payment question, ring the Tax Office on 541-766-6808. For value questions, phone Assessment at 541-766-6855.

How the bill is calculated

Each property gets a real market value from the Assessor. The tax is figured on whichever is lower: that value or the maximum assessed value. The maximum began at 1995-96 values minus 10%. Growth is limited to 3% a year, along with any value added by new improvements.

A sale does not reset the maximum, which is why neighbors in matching houses can pay very different amounts. Rates apply per $1,000 of assessed value and differ by taxing district; the districts set them, not the Assessor.

Measure 5 puts a ceiling on any one account: education taxes may not pass $5 per $1,000 of real market value, nor general government taxes $10 per $1,000. If a bill exceeds it, the amount is cut back. That cut is called compression. Compression applies only where a bill actually passes the cap.

Due dates and where to pay

One payment on November 15 covers everything, or you can split it into three: that same day, then mid-February, then mid-May. Only the single November payment earns the 3% discount. When the 15th is a Saturday or Sunday, payment is due the next business day. Overdue money collects 1.333% interest on the 16th of every month.

  • Drop box outside the Kalapuya Building (4500 SW Research Way in Corvallis).
  • In person at the Tax Office, first floor of that building.
  • Mailed with your coupon to the county's post office box 964 in Corvallis, ZIP 97339.
  • Through the county website, using a card or an e-check.
  • Phone line: 1-866-898-2918.

If taxes go unpaid

Real property tax still unpaid after May 15 is delinquent, and foreclosure becomes possible when the first delinquency reaches three years. The Tax Department moves in this order:

  • Delinquency notices mail after May 15, and interest keeps running.
  • A courtesy notice after June 15 gives payment dates that keep a property off the published list.
  • A foreclosure notice follows July 15, which is also the last day for a personal check.
  • The property list runs in the local paper in mid to late August.
  • About 30 days later a general judgment is filed with the Circuit Court, and an owner who disagrees has 30 days to answer.

A granted judgment starts a two-year redemption period. Redeeming costs the judgment's taxes and interest, a 5% penalty and 9% annual interest over the judgment period, all at once, because partial payments are refused. Nobody has to move out while the clock runs. Heirs, lienholders of record and anyone with a recorded interest on the judgment date can also redeem. When no one does, the Tax Collector deeds the property to Benton County, which may auction it. ORS chapter 312 sets these rules.

How to appeal your assessment

Appeals are heard by the Property Value Appeals Board, called BOPTA, and you file the petition with the County Clerk. The filing period opens when statements are mailed and ends December 31, or the following business day if that is a weekend or holiday.

  • In person: County Clerk's counter, second floor at 4500 SW Research Way, closing at 5 p.m. on the last day.
  • By mail: P.O. Box 888, Corvallis, OR 97339, stamped by the last day.
  • Fax or Bopta@bentoncountyor.gov, received by midnight on the last day.

The burden is yours to show the value is wrong. Evidence that helps: an arm's-length sale roughly three to six months from January 1, a recent fee appraisal, adjusted comparable sales or repair estimates. A neighbor's lower bill is not evidence.

Hearings start the first Monday in February and wrap up by April 15. Disagree with the board's order? The next venue is the Oregon Tax Court Magistrate Division, and the clock is 30 days from mailing.

Taxes and disclosure at closing

Oregon's tax year begins July 1 and ends June 30, with the lien attaching July 1. Escrow should walk you through who covers which part of this year's bill. If an older year was never paid, ask for the payoff in writing.

Older owners often run into two more topics. One is the state deferral program for seniors and people with disabilities: the state pays your county bill for you and puts a 6% lien on the house. Selling or transferring the home triggers repayment, due by August 15 of the next year, and heirs can end up responsible.

The other is the seller disclosure form. Under ORS 105.464 the form travels with a written offer, and the buyer keeps five days to back out. Court-appointed personal representatives and financial institutions that took a property in foreclosure are exempt from the full form.

Selling with taxes owed

You do not need to clear a delinquent balance before a cash sale. Escrow gets a written payoff, pays taxes and interest out of your proceeds, and records the deed. This helps most after a foreclosure notice, since the steps above stay in play until closing pays the account.

Ask who in the household can sign, and whether a lender or relative has a recorded interest. Phone the Tax Office for today's payoff and ask how far along the foreclosure timeline your account is. Then weigh a listing, with its repairs and waiting, against a written cash offer that settles the taxes at closing.

A practical checklist for Benton County sellers

Corvallis rentals and inherited houses make up a good share of local sales, so the paperwork questions tend to be the same ones. Work through them in order and you will know what a buyer or escrow officer is going to ask.

  • Confirm that this year's bill is paid and that no older year is hanging open. A single unpaid year changes how escrow prepares the payoff.
  • Check for a deferral lien if the owner was ever a senior or had a disability. That lien is paid off when the house sells.
  • Look at your last statement to see which taxing districts bill you, since districts differ from one address to the next.
  • If heirs are selling, confirm who has authority to sign. Court-appointed personal representatives get a lighter disclosure form, but a title company still wants proof of that appointment.

A cash buyer can usually work through most of these snags, though each one still needs a written payoff or a signature before funds move.

Frequently asked questions

When are Benton County property taxes due?

Taxes are due November 15 in full, or in installments on November 15, February 15 and May 15. A full payment by November 15 earns a 3% discount, and anything unpaid after May 15 is delinquent.

How long do I have to appeal my Benton County assessment?

You can file from the day statements are mailed until December 31, or the next business day if that date is a weekend or holiday. Petitions go to the County Clerk, and hearings run from the first Monday in February to April 15.

Can Benton County foreclose on my house for unpaid taxes?

Yes, once the taxes have been delinquent for three years. After a general judgment, the owner has a two-year redemption period, and the county may deed and auction the property if nobody redeems.

What happens to a senior property tax deferral when the house sells?

The deferred taxes, 6% annual interest and recording costs come due after a sale or change of ownership. Payment is due by August 15 of the following year, and the lien stays until it is paid.

Who do I call about a Benton County property tax question?

For a bill or a payment question, ring the Tax Office on 541-766-6808. For value questions, phone Assessment at 541-766-6855. Both offices are open weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Deschutes County in brief

Central Oregon's high desert is home to Deschutes County, a 3,055-square-mile county with Bend as both seat and largest city. Redmond and Sisters are the other towns most buyers know. The U.S. Forest Service owns 51% of the county's land, so privately owned land is limited, and that scarcity shapes local property values.

Population grew from 115,367 in 2000 to 198,253 in 2020. Tourism, retail, forest products, recreational equipment, aviation and technology make up the economy, and destination resorts such as Sunriver, Eagle Crest and Pronghorn are among the ten largest taxpayers.

Zoning on rural land falls to the county's Community Development Department. What a parcel lets a buyer build or rent can change its worth to them, so confirm it before a sale.

Cold, dry weather and your house

Bend sits at 3,628 feet and gets about 12 inches of precipitation a year, with average temperatures of 30.5 in January and 65.5 in July. Winters are real, and houses face stresses unknown in western Oregon:

  • snow load on roofs and ice dams along the eaves
  • freeze and thaw cycles that crack driveways, patios and foundations
  • wood decks and siding that dry and split in the summer sun
  • heating systems and well or septic equipment that must handle cold snaps

A vacant house that went through a winter without heat can need real work before a lender will finance a buyer's purchase of it.

Deschutes County tax figures

Taxing districts imposed about $560.4 million in property tax for fiscal year 2024-25 on $33.74 billion of assessed value. The average rate was $16.61 per $1,000 of assessed value, with a Measure 5 rate of $6.76 per $1,000 of Measure 5 value.

Reading and paying your tax bill

Statements go online in the county's Dial system by October 20 and are mailed by October 25 each fall. The Property Tax office asks owners to correct a mailing address before September 30. A paper statement includes instructions for switching to email.

Color helps with escrow. A yellow statement means a lender is paying the taxes, and a green one means no lender is.

Payment routes, with fees to confirm before you pay:

  • Mail to Deschutes County Tax Collector, PO Box 7559, Bend, OR 97708-7559.
  • Online at deschutes.org/tax, or by phone at (866) 871-5856 at any hour.
  • A 24-hour drop box at 1300 NW Wall Street in Bend, and a Redmond box at 411 SW 9th Street open only in set windows before each due date.
  • Bank bill pay, with a separate payment for each account using its six-digit account number.

Keep a hand-stamped USPS receipt, because mail postmarks are applied at a distribution center. Schedule bank payments well ahead, since they can arrive days late.

Unpaid taxes and foreclosure

After three years of delinquency, Oregon allows foreclosure on real property. The county then holds the property for two years while the owner and lienholders can redeem it. ORS chapter 312 sets those periods, a 5% penalty and a redemption fee.

Deschutes County has sold foreclosed properties at auction. Recent years show the scale: 37 parcels for $1,115,060 in 2018, 34 parcels for $640,100 in 2019, 30 parcels for $768,100 in 2020, 12 parcels for $1,336,000 in 2021, and 16 parcels for $702,600 in 2022.

An owner who is behind has the most options before the three-year mark arrives, and a sale before foreclosure keeps whatever equity exists in your hands.

How to appeal your assessment

Only the County Clerk's Office can accept petitions. Mail them to P.O. Box 6005, Bend, OR 97708-6005, or deliver them to 1300 NW Wall Street, Suite 202. Postmarks are acceptable.

State law sets the deadline at December 31, moved to the next business day when it falls on a weekend or holiday. The board meets from the first Monday in February to March 15.

For value questions before you file, call the Assessor at 541-388-6508 or email appraisal@deschutes.org. The Dial site also offers a tax estimator and a rate lookup by account.

Short-term rentals

Some Deschutes County houses are run as short-term rentals. In unincorporated Deschutes County, transient room tax rules in County Code Chapter 4.08 apply to overnight rentals of up to 30 consecutive days. Paying that tax does not amount to land use approval.

Any structure used as a rental must meet land use, building and onsite wastewater rules, and eligibility can depend on whether the dwelling was lawfully established. If you run a rental, confirm its status with the Community Development Department before you list it as one.

Deferral and disclosure

Older owners may have a senior or disabled deferral. When the home sells, the balance with 6% interest is due by August 15 of the next year. The late-filing fee is 10% of the last tax bill, from $20 to $180.

ORS 105.464 requires the seller disclosure with a written offer, and the buyer has five days to revoke.

Before you list: records to gather

Start with your latest statement and note its color. If it is yellow, a lender pays through escrow and will send a payoff request at closing. If it is green, you pay directly, so confirm every installment is current. Next, pull the Dial record for your account number and compare the assessed value with the real market value.

Then walk the property the way an inspector would. Look at the roof edge for ice dam damage, the foundation and driveway for cracks, and the deck and siding for splitting. Photograph anything you have repaired and keep receipts, since a buyer's lender will ask about winter condition on a house that sat empty.

Selling with taxes owed

A cash sale lets the title company pay the county from your proceeds, so a balance does not stop the closing. Ask the Property Tax office for a payoff on your target date, and ask whether a deferral lien is recorded.

If the property is a rental or sits on rural land, say so up front. Those details, plus snow damage or an unheated winter, are what a buyer prices in, and a cash offer that accounts for them saves you the repair bills and showings a listing would need.

Frequently asked questions

When do Deschutes County property tax statements come out?

Statements appear online in Dial by October 20 and are mailed by October 25. The county asks owners to fix a wrong mailing address by September 30.

Where do I pay property taxes in Deschutes County?

You can pay online at deschutes.org/tax, by phone, by mail to PO Box 7559, Bend, in a drop box or in person at 1300 NW Wall Street, Suite 203. Weekday hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

What does a yellow property tax statement mean in Deschutes County?

A yellow statement means a lender is paying the taxes through an escrow account, and a green one means no lender is.

How do I appeal my Deschutes County assessment?

File a petition with the County Clerk at 1300 NW Wall Street, Suite 202, or by mail to PO Box 6005, Bend. The state deadline is December 31, moved to the next business day when it falls on a weekend or holiday.

Do short-term rental owners in Deschutes County owe a lodging tax?

Owners of overnight rentals in unincorporated areas owe the transient room tax under County Code Chapter 4.08. The tax is not land use approval, so a separate review may still apply.
